paras: The killing of Wilson Edwards was the fatal shooting of a Black prisoner by a member of a sheriff's posse in the jail at Monroe, North Carolina, in late May 1882. Edwards, held on a peace warrant, was shot as Sheriff A. J. Price and a group of helpers tried to put him in irons, and a coroner's jury found the shooting justifiable. North Carolina papers printed detailed accounts from the officers' side, and a short wire item carried the story to Tennessee, Alabama and Missouri as the death of 'a notorious desperado'.

According to the Monroe Enquirer, Edwards, of Sandy Ridge Township, had been jailed at the close of the Superior Court term for want of bondsmen on a peace warrant sworn out by a Black woman he had allegedly tried to shoot. The Richmond State, as summarized in the Western Sentinel, said he grew desperate when told he would stay in jail until court time, tore planks from the ceiling and threatened to kill the sheriff. In that version a magistrate told the sheriff to take him from the cell and chain him in the dungeon.

The Enquirer wrote that on a Wednesday Edwards refused his dinner and cursed the sheriff, who decided he should be ironed and sent for three or four Black men and then several white men, among them J. E. W. Austin, John S. Richardson, B. H. Binford, E. T. Wade and Robert Simpson. Rather than enter the cell, they opened the door to overpower him as he came out, but he rushed out with a stick in each hand. Ben Blakeney, a Black helper, was struck in the mouth, Simpson had two fingers broken, and Binford was hit on the neck and followed into an opposite dungeon.

There, by the Enquirer's account, three shots were fired, and Richardson pulled Edwards to the floor by a handkerchief around his neck. The Richmond State said Binford shot him as he was about to strike again, and that one ball, smaller than those from Binford's .32 pistol, was thought to have been fired by someone else. Edwards died in less than an hour, with wounds through the liver and kidney.

The coroner's jury returned a verdict that the killing was in self-defense and justifiable, naming Binford as the shooter in the version given by the Richmond State. The Enquirer added the sheriff's report that a former fellow prisoner said Edwards had planned to feign insanity and escape, and claimed he had earlier shot Jack Huneycutt. No report of any further proceedings appears in the coverage.

The local account, reprinted from the Monroe Enquirer in the Charlotte Home and Democrat on June 2, called Edwards 'a dangerous customer' and 'a desperate character' and concluded that 'no blame can be attached to any one'. The Western Sentinel of Winston ran the Richmond State version on June 1 under the heading 'Killing of a Prisoner', repeating the posse's account and the verdict without comment but placing the event in 'Moore county'.

Out of state, a two-sentence wire item calling him 'Willis Edwards, a notorious desperado' appeared in the Milan Exchange and the Huntsville Gazette on June 3 and the Iron County Register on June 8. No Black-press account was available for this period, and no report gave Edwards's own side or questioned the officers' version.

The local paper named him Wilson and gave his age as 30 or 35, while the Richmond State and the wire called him Willis and the Richmond State put him at about 25. The Enquirer did not name the shooter, while the Richmond State and the verdict it quoted named Binford, and the wire said four men were wounded where the Enquirer named three.

reader.title: Killing of Wilson Edwards
bases: A jailed prisoner was shot dead by a member of a sheriff's posse while the sheriff and his helpers tried to put him in irons (A1, A2, A5).

The Monroe Enquirer account (A2) and the Richmond State account summarized in A1 agree on the jail, the peace warrant, the attempt to subdue him, the injuries to Binford and Simpson, his death within an hour and the coroner's verdict, though both come from the officers' side.

accounts.label: Monroe Enquirer (local)
accounts.gist: Edwards, thought deranged and later said to have planned to 'play off crazy' and escape, attacked the sheriff's helpers with sticks; three shots were fired as he beat Binford, and no blame attached to anyone.

accounts.label: Richmond State (via Western Sentinel)
accounts.gist: Edwards raved, tore planks from the ceiling and threatened to kill; a posse sent on a magistrate's order tried to take him, and Binford shot him in self-defence while being struck, with a fourth, smaller ball possibly fired by someone else.

accounts.label: Wire report
accounts.gist: A 'notorious desperado' was killed in the Monroe jail in an affray with the sheriff and posse after wounding four men.

framing.detail: The Enquirer, reprinted in Charlotte, called him 'a dangerous customer' and 'a desperate character' and held that it 'became necessary to fire on him'.
The Richmond State summary under 'Killing of a Prisoner' gave the posse's version and the self-defence verdict without question.
Out-of-state papers ran a two-sentence wire item calling him 'a notorious desperado'.

conflicts.note: The local Monroe Enquirer gives Wilson; the Richmond State and the wire give Willis.

versions.value: Monroe, i.e. Union County (Monroe Enquirer; 'Monroe Court-house')

conflicts.note: A1's 'Moore county' is likely an error; its details (Binford, Simpson, peace warrant, verdict) match the Monroe account.

versions.value: Binford shot him twice; another ball, smaller than Binford's .32, thought fired by some other party

conflicts.note: The coroner's verdict as given in A1 names Binford.

record_check.dossier: Before May 29, 1882 (reported by the Richmond State of the 29th); the Enquirer's 'Wednesday' points to May 24.
One victim with two spellings of his first name (Wilson locally, Willis in the Richmond State and wire).
Sheriff A. J. Price's posse; B. H. Binford named by the coroner's jury as the shooter.
Held on a peace warrant for trying to shoot a woman; also alleged to have shot Jack Huneycutt.
Shooting and killing by the posse; the beating was by Edwards of his captors, per their account.

record_check.record: Sheriff Price and several white men entered his cell
record_check.dossier: They opened the door to overpower him as he came out; the shooting happened in the corridor or an opposite dungeon.

info: Not stated as a date; the Monroe Enquirer says 'On Wednesday', and the Richmond State account summarized in the Western Sentinel ran on the 29th, so the killing came before May 29, 1882 (probably Wednesday, May 24).
The jail at Monroe (Monroe Court-house), N.C.
Wilson Edwards (Monroe Enquirer) or Willis Edwards (Richmond State, wire), described as 'colored' and a 'negro', of Sandy Ridge Township, aged 30 or 35 (A2) or about 25 (A1).
Jailed for want of bondsmen on a peace warrant sworn out by a Black woman he was said to have tried to shoot; the Enquirer added that he was the person who had shot Jack Huneycutt.
Sheriff A. J. Price and a posse of Black and white men; B. H. Binford fired the shots per the coroner's verdict (A1); the Enquirer says three shots were fired without naming the shooter (A2).
